name: Yucatec Maya
confidence_why: Yucatec is a tone language by every instrumental account (Kügler, Skopeteas & Verhoeven 2007; Sobrino Gómez 2013; Kidder 2013), but whether it also has word stress is openly contested: Bricker, Po'ot Yah & Dzul de Po'ot 1998 put stress on the long vowel or else the final syllable, Gussenhoven & Teeuw 2008 on long syllables and a word-initial short syllable, Andrade 1955 calls accent lexical, Kidder 2013 finds no obligatory word-level stress at all, and DiCanio & Bennett 2018 conclude there is little consensus.

sweep_summary: Eight title hits for Yucatec Maya (yuca1254; catalog: tonal, deciding source Kidder 2013 dissertation, open text held by the project). Only one item could be newly obtained and read: Kügler, Skopeteas & Verhoeven 2007 (ISIS 8, pp. 187-208), downloaded as the whole-volume PDF from the SFB 632 site and. it is an instrumental tone/information-structure study ('Yucatec Maya is a tone language, displaying a three-fold opposition'; long vowels obligatorily H or L, short vowels toneless; no intonational focus marking) and says nothing about word-stress placement, so it confirms the tonal coding and is silent on stress. Kidder's 2013 Benjamins chapter 'Stress in Yucatec Maya' is paywalled (Crossref abstract read: 'no detailed account of stress.. has been made'; the chapter is the Spanish-loanword diagnostic already contained in her open dissertation), priority low. McQuown 1975 'El acento del maya yucateco' (Lima, Instituto de Estudios Peruanos; pp. 59-71) is print-only (HathiTrust search-only, OCLC 7992974); Sobrino Gómez 2013 cites it among binary H/L tone analyses, so it is probably a tone statement; priority medium; Glottolog's 'Matos & Ravines 1975' is a duplicate record of the same paper under the volume editors' names. Uth 2018 and the two Michnowicz & Hyler 2020 chapters concern Yucatan Spanish prosody/rhythm (abstracts read via Crossref), and Redzich 2011 is medieval German philology (Glottolog mis-association) - all irrelevant to Maya word stress. The best first-hand stress statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Andrade 1955 §1.6 (already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16; re-read): accent lexically determined, dominant final accent in disyllables, penult accent when the penult has a long vowel, always-final in 4+ syllable words - the same shape as the Bricker et al. 1998 default that Kidder reviews; it refines the catalog's record of competing proposals but does not supersede Kidder 2013. Nothing found contradicts the 'tonal' coding. Benjamins, HathiTrust search, publishup and Bielefeld behind bot walls; web.archive.org unreachable.

new_statements.quote: Accent in Modern Yucatec appears to be determined lexically; with few exceptions, a sharp division can be made between those verbs in which the stem is accented, regardless of whether one, two, or more suffixes are added, and those whose stem is invariably unaccented. Regarding nouns, somewhat more complex behavior is noted. [...] (a) The most frequent pattern for disyllabic noun and verb forms is that in which the ultima bears the accent. [...] (b) The accent falls on the penult in a small number of nouns and verbs; and in all words which contain a double vowel in the penult. [...] In the relatively few words in the texts which contain more than three syllables, the ultima is invariably accented
new_statements.citation: Andrade, Manuel J. 1955. A Grammar of Modern Yucatec. Microfilm Collection of Manuscripts on Middle American Cultural Anthropology, Series 7, No. 41. University of Chicago Library (manuscript completed before 1941, released by N. A. McQuown); online edition by Christian Lehmann. Section 1.6 'Accent'.
new_statements.reading: The earliest first-hand descriptive account (1930s field texts): word accent is lexically fixed per stem, with final accent as the dominant disyllabic pattern, penult accent whenever the penult holds a long ('double') vowel, and invariable final accent in words of four or more syllables. In shape this is the same default that Bricker, Po'ot Yah & Dzul de Po'ot 1998 later state (stress the long vowel, otherwise the final syllable), but Andrade frames it as lexical with exceptions and notes that greater stress often accompanies lower pitch, i.e. stress is not identified with high tone. It adds a pre-Kidder first-hand data point on the 'stress is lexical/unpredictable' side of the debate the catalog already records; it does not overturn Kidder 2013's instrumental finding of no obligatory word-level stress pattern.

new_statements.quote: Accent. This is not marked. It is in part dependent upon the length of the vowel. Contracted syllables usually seem to have greater stress of voice laid upon them. In spite of some authorities to the contrary, there seem to be few cases where a difference in accent occasions a difference in the meaning of the form.1 The accent in all the Lacandone chants is much more noticeable than in the ordinary speech. There is often a definite rhythm and in the slow chants this is very marked.2 [fn. 1:] I was unable to find the distinction in accent made by Beltran (§ 98) between the infinitive of certain verbs in -l and the past participle; lub-ul, to fall and lub-ul, a thing fallen, lik-il, to raise and lik-il, a thing raised.

new_statements.relation_note: Refines rather than settles. The catalog codes Yucatec as tonal-OR-pitch accent with word stress disputed (Kidder 2013: no obligatory word-level stress; Bricker et al. 1998 default = leftmost long vowel, else final). Tozzer 1921 is a pre-tone-era source: he says nothing about pitch, gives no position rule, and only notes that accent tracks vowel length in part and that contracted syllables sound stressed, while doubting that accent is contrastive. The 'in part dependent upon the length of the vowel' clause is compatible with the long-vowel-attracts-stress side (Bricker et al; Andrade's penult accent on long vowels) and with Kidder's reinterpretation of early 'accent' as a length/tone effect…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tozzer gives no placement rule. He does not mark accent in his transcription, says it depends 'in part' on vowel length (i.e. long vowels attract it) and that contracted syllables seem to carry more stress, and holds that accent is almost never distinctive (contrasts in meaning by accent alone are few), explicitly failing to hear Beltrán's infinitive/participle accent minimal pairs (lubul, likil). Chant accent is more prominent and rhythmic than in ordinary speech.
new_statements.exceptions: 'few cases' of meaning distinguished by accent, said to be claimed by 'some authorities' (Beltrán § 98 on -l infinitive vs. participle) but not found by Tozzer; Lacandone chant rhythm differs from ordinary speech
new_statements.identity_note: Tozzer 1921 covers the Maya spoken around Valladolid, Yucatan, and notes the Lacandone (Chiapas) dialect as 'essentially the same' apart from a few phonetic changes and less contraction; his chant-accent remark is specifically about Lacandone chants. Nothing dialect-specific was read for Krämer 2001 or McQuown 1975.

new_statements.rule_in_words: McQuown analyses Yucatec 'acento' as a property of every syllable, a bundle of pitch (alto/-ascendente, mediano-neutral, bajo/-descendente), glottality, quantity, quality and intensity: syllables carry high accent (/á/ /áa/), low accent (/à/ /àa/) or neutral tone (/a/), and these contrasts distinguish lexical items and grammatical categories (p. 62). Intensity is not an independent word stress: Figura 2 ranks the 12 syllable types by intensity, from 1 CV́Vʔ and 2 CV́V (high tone, long) through the low-tone types 7-10 (CV̀Vʔ, CV̀V, CV̀ʔ, CV̀) down to the toneless 11-12 (CVʔ, CV), i.e. prominence follows tone and vowel length/glottalization. Placement is stated only at the phrase level (Figura 3): the intonational nucleus (greatest intensity) is selected by that hierarchy, and within the compilation of two or more equal accents (all high or all low) the primary stress is the PENULTIMATE accented syllable of the compilation; the other accented syllables get secondary stress, mid/neutral-tone syllables tertiary, except that the phrase-final syllable also gets secondary stress and a syllable under paralinguistic contrastive intensity attracts the phrase's main intensity. No rule places stress by position in the word; earlier proposals (Andrade: stress correlating with double/long vowels or the final syllable; Blair 1964: an intensity pulse on the initial syllable of a stretch and on alternate syllables) are reported as prior attempts, not adopted.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, derived: in the compilation of equal (high or low) accents the non-penultimate accented syllables carry secondary stress (marked); the phrase-final syllable also carries secondary stress; syllables with neutral (mid) tone carry tertiary stress (p. 65). Blair's 1964 alternating intensity pulse (initial syllable of a stretch and alternate syllables thereafter, with two exceptions) is summarised on p. 61 as an earlier proposal.
new_statements.exceptions: (p. 65) the last syllable of the phrase receives secondary rather than tertiary stress; a syllable bearing paralinguistic contrastive intensity attracts the greatest intensity of the phrase regardless of the hierarchy; (p. 61, after Blair) an accented syllable lengthens except before /ʔ/; phrase-final accents fall under the terminal intonation contours and are treated separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Modern spoken Yucatec Maya: McQuown's system is built on the tape-recorded conversations of Blair & Vermont Salas, Spoken Yucatec Maya (Chicago 1965/1967; speaker Refugio Vermont Salas), with examples also from the Motul dictionary (Ciudad Real c. 1580) and Andrade's 1930s texts; his own 1949 fieldwork covered Valladolid, Dzilam González and Xocempich (Yucatán) and Ich Ek and Becal (Campeche). Paper read at the XXXIX International Congress of Americanists, Lima 1970, printed 1975.

new_statements.quote: These data show that Yucatec Maya is quantity-sensitive with coda consonants being moraic and thus contributing to the weight of a syllable. [...] From the accent distribution data and Fisher's measurements, I conclude that in Yucatec Maya, trochaic bimoraic symmetric feet are built. [...] What can be observed in the data in (23, 24) is that an accented foot is built at the right and at the left edge of a phrase or word. Heavy (CVC, CVV or heavier) syllables attract stress. Thus, Yucatec Maya has initial stress. Final stress arises by the interaction of the requirement to have a closed (CVC) syllable at the right word edge and the stress-to-weight principle, which also assigns stress to medial syllables in case they are heavy.

It is compatible with the catalog's classification of the language as tonal with a disputed stress system; as a stress claim it sits on the opposite side from Kidde…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Krämer (working from Blair & Vermont-Salas 1967 intonation-superscript transcriptions plus Fisher 1976's pitch measurements, and noting on p. 188 that 'Unfortunately, no work is done so far on the accentual system' but that quantity-sensitivity is 'uncontroversial among Mayanists' per Pfeiler p.c.) analyses Yucatec as quantity-sensitive with moraic codas and trochaic bimoraic feet: a foot is built at both the left and the right edge of the word/phrase, so the initial syllable is stressed and the final syllable (always closed, hence heavy, because every word ends in a consonant, with glottal-stop/h epenthesis otherwise) is stressed; word-medial heavy syllables (CVV, CVC) are also stressed/footed, word-medial light syllables are unfooted; two initial light syllables group into one (CV.CV) foot. He does not rank these stresses as primary vs secondary. He treats lexical high vs low/neutral tone on long vowels as given ('phonemic pitch accent, i.e. high and low or neutral tone', fn. 9: Mayanists disagree which tone is marked 'if it is a tone system at all') and says a high-toned syllable before the final gets higher/more intense intonation than the final, 'which is still stressed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit primary/secondary ranking: both word edges carry an accented foot and medial heavy syllables are 'stressed or footed'; the final syllable 'always has a higher intonation than neutral', and a preceding high-toned syllable outranks it intonationally.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-medial light (CV) syllables are unaccented/unfooted (ex. 24c); fn. 10: 'In phrases containing tone bearing morphemes, stress assignment is a little more complicated' and tone-bearing material is excluded from the data; the stress excursus is explicitly provisional ('no work is done so far on the accentual system') and serves the vowel-harmony argument (coda moraicity), the foot being declared irrelevant to harmony.
new_statements.identity_note: Krämer names no dialect; his data are second-hand (Blair & Vermont-Salas 1967, Ayres & Pfeiler 1997, Fisher 1976). The catalog's B check notes the H/L tone contrast is described specifically for the Western dialect (Kidder 2013 sec. 3.6 after Frazier 2009).

tone_statements.quote: Dejando de lado por ahora la discusión del tono de las vocales rearticuladas, existe acuerdo en que las vocales modales largas del maya yucateco portan tono, existiendo en la lengua un inventario tonal básico de dos tonos que contrastan; tono bajo y tono alto (Fisher 1973; Fox 1978; Frazier 2011; Sobrino Gómez 2013). ... En palabras en aislamiento, los tonos fonológicos manifiestan varias realizaciones fonéticas. El tono alto muestra un descenso, tanto en palabras monosilábicas como en la segunda sílaba de palabras bisilábicas.
tone_statements.translation: Leaving aside for now the discussion of the tone of the rearticulated vowels, there is agreement that the long modal vowels of Yucatec Maya carry tone, the language having a basic tonal inventory of two contrasting tones; low tone and high tone (Fisher 1973; Fox 1978; Frazier 2011; Sobrino Gómez 2013). ... In words in isolation, the phonological tones show several phonetic realisations. The high tone shows a fall, both in monosyllabic words and in the second syllable of disyllabic words.
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones, high vs low, only on long modal vowels; high realised as falling, low level or rising. Purely tonal morphemes posited (derivational H, stative L, middle voice H, antipassive L). Pitch tracks shown. Stress stated separately: iambic; long vowels attract it.

tone_statements.quote: YM utilizes a four-way contrast on the basis of length, tone, and glottalization. ... In (2), we see the four vowel shapes (SHORT, LOW TONE, HIGH TONE, and GLOTTALIZED) as commonly described in the literature. ... v SHORT: short, unmarked for tone, modal voice ... v̀v LOW TONE: long, low tone, modal voice ... v́v HIGH TONE: long, high tone, modal voice ... v́ʔv GLOTTALIZED: two short vowels (the first with high tone) interrupted by a glottal stop ... The SHORT vowel is described as having neutral tone, meaning SHORT vowels do not participate in a tonal contrast (B&VS: 7)

tone_statements.summary: High vs low tone on long vowels only (short vowels toneless, glottalized vowels start high). tone_statements.citation: Blair, Robert Wallace. 1964. Yucatec Maya noun and verb morpho-syntax. PhD dissertation, Indiana University, Bloomington (University Microfilms, Ann Arbor; Sobrino 2013 cites the microfilm as 1966).
tone_statements.quote: Yucatec Maya (a Mayan language of Mexico, henceforth abbreviated as YM) is one of the few Mayan languages to use a tonal contrast. Long vowels are produced with either low tone (e.g. /mìis/ cat) or high tone (e.g. /míis/ sweep). There is also a third type of long vowel used in YM; GLOTTALIZED vowels are produced with initial high pitch and with creaky voice. ... there is a four-way contrast of suprasegmental features, henceforth referred to as vowel shape. ... Thus, SHORT vowels are the only vowels not marked for tone; all long vowels bear some tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1 Introduction, ms p. 1, and sec. 2 Production of Vowel Contrasts in Yucatec Maya, ms p. 2
tone_statements.summary: Two tones (low, high) on long vowels; short vowels toneless; four 'vowel shapes' SHORT /v/, LOW TONE /v̀v/, HIGH TONE /v́v/, GLOTTALIZED /v́v̰/ (Bricker et al. 1998); fn. 18: GLOTTALIZED vowels also phonologically high-toned. F0, duration, glottalization measured; perception tests. No word stress.

readall_conflicts: Only one of the three works could be read. Tozzer 1921 (p. 27) does not contradict anything in the catalog: he gives no placement rule, ties accent partly to vowel length, adds an impression that contracted syllables are stressed, and doubts accent is contrastive, refusing Beltrán's infinitive/participle accent pairs. That mild 'accent is rarely distinctive' stance sits alongside Andrade 1955's 'accent is determined lexically' statement already held by the project and Kidder 2013's instrumental finding of no obligatory word stress, versus the Bricker et al. 1998 / Gussenhoven & Teeuw 2008 / Krämer 2001 rule-based proposals the catalog records second-hand through Kidder. Krämer 2001 (bot wall) and McQuown 1975 (HathiTrust search-only) remain unread, so the Krämer stress claim (initial and final syllables plus intervening heavy syllables, trochaic bimoraic feet) is still carried only through Kidder 2013 and cannot be checked against its own text. sources.quote: Yucatec Maya (a Mayan language of Mexico, henceforth abbreviated as YM) is one of the few Mayan languages to use a tonal contrast. Long vowels are produced with either low tone (e.g. /mìis/ cat) or high tone (e.g. /míis/ sweep). There is also a third type of long vowel used in YM; GLOTTALIZED vowels are produced with initial high pitch and with creaky voice. ... there is a four-way contrast of suprasegmental features, henceforth referred to as vowel shape. ... Thus, SHORT vowels are the only vowels not marked for tone; all long vowels bear some tone.

tone.quote: YM utilizes a four-way contrast on the basis of length, tone, and glottalization. ... In (2), we see the four vowel shapes (SHORT, LOW TONE, HIGH TONE, and GLOTTALIZED) as commonly described in the literature. ... v SHORT: short, unmarked for tone, modal voice ... v̀v LOW TONE: long, low tone, modal voice ... v́v HIGH TONE: long, high tone, modal voice ... v́ʔv GLOTTALIZED: two short vowels (the first with high tone) interrupted by a glottal stop ... The SHORT vowel is described as having neutral tone, meaning SHORT vowels do not participate in a tonal contrast (B&VS: 7)
tone.locator: sec. 1 (Yucatec Maya background), pp. 2-3 of the author's
tone.summary: High vs low tone on long vowels only (short vowels toneless, glottalized vowels start high). Acoustic study, 24 speakers: HIGH surfaces as a fall, LOW level low; Mérida/Santa Elena keep the contrast, in Sisbicchén 'tone is not phonemic'. Grammatical tone on verbs noted in passing. Nothing on stress.
